title: A Centenary of Justice -- Ch. 2: Old Doctrines and New Paradigms
primary_topics: Chapter 2 of 'A Centenary of Justice' -- CJP's Centenary Lecture Series lecture (Feb 13, 2001, SC Session Hall) on how the Court used traditional legal doctrines to meet new 'e-age' paradigms across four domains: the new economy, constitutional law, political law and medical malpractice

Premise: in the e-age, judges need both liberal education and legal expertise; quoting Learned Hand, a constitutional judge must have 'a bowing acquaintance' with history, literature and philosophy because well-rounded judgment, not mere doctrinal mastery, is essential

The new economy (globalization, liberalization, deregulation, privatization): Tanada v. Angara (WTO upheld on grave-abuse deference; non-self-executing 'Filipino First'); Tatad v. Secretary of Energy (Oil Deregulation Law RA 8180 voided for entrenching the Big Three oligopoly); Garcia v. Corona (the corrected RA 8479 upheld); fiscal decentralization (Pimentel v. Aguirre)

New paradigms in constitutional and political law (free expression/exit polls, libel, the death penalty, due process for workers and extraditees, privacy, citizenship, automated elections, initiative/referendum/recall, the party-list formula, the environment, EDSA II) and medical malpractice (res ipsa loquitur)
sub_topics: Liberal education and legal expertise: 'It is no longer enough for judges to be walking encyclopedias of the Constitution'; they must also grasp economics, biotechnology, computers and the sciences -- anchored in Judge Learned Hand's portrait of the ideal magistrate

Tanada v. Angara (WTO): the Senate's concurrence did not violate the non-self-executing economic-nationalism/'Filipino First' provisions; upheld on the old doctrine of deference -- petitioners failed to show grave abuse; 'Constitutions... should be interpreted to cover even future and unknown circumstances'

Manila Prince Hotel v. GSIS distinguished: Section 10, Art. XII held self-executing (Filipino bidder may match a winning foreign bid) but only as to the national economy and patrimony, 'exceptions rather than the rule'

Tatad v. Secretary of Energy (deregulation): RA 8180 voided 9-2 (Puno, J.) for three provisions (tariff differential, minimum inventory, predatory pricing) that entrenched the Petron-Shell-Caltex oligopoly; 'the Constitution mandates this Court to be the guardian not only of the people's political rights but their economic rights as well'; the Court struck the law's craft, not the policy of deregulation
Garcia v. Corona: the corrected Oil Deregulation Law (RA 8479) upheld unanimously -- 'what constitutes reasonable time is not for judicial determination'

Decentralization: Pimentel v. Aguirre (LGU fiscal autonomy; automatic IRA release; AO 372 partially void); Drilon v. Lim (President has supervision, not control, over LGUs); Ganzon; Meralco v. Province of Laguna

Free expression: ABS-CBN v. Comelec (exit polls are protected speech; Comelec gravely abused its discretion banning them, subject to narrowly tailored regulation); Vasquez v. CA (truth plus actual-malice standard for libel of public officials)

The death penalty and the right to life: People v. Echegaray upheld RA 7659; CJP's Dissent argued the 1987 Constitution abolished (not merely suspended) the death penalty and that Congress failed the 'heinousness' and 'compelling reasons' tests; the irreversibility of executions (Echegaray executed Feb 5, 1999) vs. corrected sentences in Gallo and De los Santos; Estrada's Dec 2000 commutation announcement; People v. Genosa remanded to receive expert testimony on the 'battered woman syndrome'

Due process paradigms: Serrano v. NLRC (CJP Dissent: dismissal without notice violates constitutional due process and warrants reinstatement, not mere back wages; due process binds private power too, not only government); Secretary of Justice v. Lantion and Jimenez (extradition due process; 9-6 ruling later reversed 9-6 on reconsideration)

Privacy and citizenship: Ople v. Torres (national ID void; right to privacy in 'clear and present danger'); Frivaldo (repatriation; citizenship needed only at assumption of office); Mercado (dual citizenship allowed, distinguished from proscribed dual allegiance); the 'reluctant hinges' of citizenship

Elections and people power: Loong v. Comelec (manual recount of automated ballots in Sulu; CJP Dissent); Bush v. Gore as comparative reference; Santiago v. Comelec and PIRMA v. Comelec (RA 6735 inadequate for a constitutional-amendment initiative); recall doctrine; Veterans Federation Party v. Comelec (the four party-list parameters -- 20% allocation, 2% threshold, 3-seat limit, proportional representation -- 'the Philippine style party list system is a unique paradigm,' rejecting the German Niemeyer formula)

Environment and EDSA II and medical malpractice: Oposa v. Factoran and Tano v. Socrates (intergenerational ecology); the Court's role in swearing in President Arroyo on Jan 20, 2001 (kept guarded under the sub judice rule); Batiquin and Ramos v. CA applying res ipsa loquitur to medical negligence
signature_phrases: It is no longer enough for judges to be walking encyclopedias of the Constitution, the codes and judicial doctrines
Constitutions are designed to meet not only the vagaries of contemporary events. They should be interpreted to cover even future and unknown circumstances
the Constitution mandates this Court to be the guardian not only of the people's political rights but their economic rights as well
the Court did not condemn the economic policy of deregulation as unconstitutional
The Philippine style party list system is a unique paradigm which demands an equally unique formula
one cannot grow Washington apples in the Philippines or Guimaras mangoes in the Arctic
Errors in its imposition become nightmarishly irreversible once the appellant is executed

stances.claim: Justices need not be economists, physicians or theologians to decide cases in those fields; the binding force of a decision does not depend on the ponente's technical expertise, because 'it is up to the parties concerned to enlighten the Court.' The judicial answer to 'the Court has no competence to decide economic issues' is that competence is supplied by adversarial argument, not by the judge's prior specialization.
stances.rhetorical_move: adversarial-competence argument: judicial authority over technical subjects justified by the party-driven nature of the process rather than by the judge's own expertise
stances.confidence: asserted firmly as a defense of judicial review over economic and scientific matters

stances.claim: The 1987 Constitution abolished -- not merely suspended -- the death penalty, creating a new right against capital punishment as a species of the right to life; any reviving statute must be strictly construed against the State and must prove 'heinousness' and 'compelling reasons' for each crime. RA 7659 and the Echegaray majority failed this test and ignored the worldwide abolition trend, and executions are 'nightmarishly irreversible.'
stances.rhetorical_move: abolition-not-suspension reading plus irreversibility argument: a structural constitutional interpretation reinforced by the practical finality of executions and the global abolitionist trend
stances.confidence: asserted as CJP's dissenting position, openly acknowledged as not the majority view

stances.claim: Due process binds not only the government but private power as well; in the e-age of globalization and deregulation, where state power has shrunk and 'corporate behemoths' operate across borders, confining the due process clause to government action (as the Serrano majority did) turns a blind eye to the real modern sources of abuse against constitutional rights.
stances.rhetorical_move: due-process-against-private-power: extending a traditionally state-limiting guarantee to private actors by reading it against the structural shift of power from state to market
stances.confidence: asserted as CJP's dissenting position in Serrano

notable_anecdotes: The 36-volume reading: CJP notes in a footnote that to write the Tanada v. Angara ponencia he had to read the entire 36-volume Uruguay Round of Multilateral Trade Negotiations plus treatises on globalization -- a concrete illustration of his liberal-education-plus-expertise thesis.

Washington apples and Guimaras mangoes: rejecting the German Niemeyer party-list formula, CJP wrote that 'one cannot grow Washington apples in the Philippines or Guimaras mangoes in the Arctic,' because the Philippine three-seat-limit, non-mandatory-20% model differs fundamentally from the German Bundestag's.

The Echegaray irreversibility: CJP contrasts Leo Echegaray -- executed February 5, 1999 -- with Gallo and De los Santos, whose death sentences were reopened and corrected after the Court found the qualifying relationship had not been alleged in the Information; 'human reversals do not affect the graveyard.'

The 'reluctant hinges' lineage: CJP recalls his political-law professor, former CA Justice Delfin Fl. Batacan, teaching 'more than forty years ago' that the doors to Philippine citizenship must open on 'reluctant hinges' -- a phrase he carries into his own jurisprudence.
target_audience: The Centenary Lecture Series audience (judges, lawyers and the legal intelligentsia) at the SC Session Hall
Bench and bar studying how settled doctrine adapts to new-economy and e-age problems
Law students and academics (the lecture doubles as a jurisprudential survey)
register_markers: doctrinal lecture register -- heavily case-cited (footnoted), four-domain survey, first-person ponente/dissenter commentary
liberal-education-plus-expertise as the governing framing premise
self-disclosed dissents (death penalty, Serrano, Lantion, Loong) marking the candid, non-triumphalist register
paean-to-the-Constitution (Tanada quotation) as the doxological coda
decision_framework_signals: grave-abuse-deference: economic-policy statutes upheld unless petitioners show patent, gross arbitrariness (Tanada; Garcia v. Corona) -- the prosperity-side deferential standard
guardian-of-economic-rights: the Court will still strike economic laws that violate the Constitution's fair-competition mandate (Tatad) -- deference is not abdication
adversarial-competence: judicial authority over technical fields supplied by party argument, not judicial specialization
abolition-not-suspension + irreversibility: the death-penalty dissent's structural-plus-practical reasoning
due-process-against-private-power: constitutional guarantees extended to private actors in a deregulated, globalized economy
unique-paradigm-unique-formula: rejecting wholesale transplantation of foreign models (Niemeyer) to Philippine conditions
one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 2 of 'A Centenary of Justice' reproduces the Centenary Lecture Series lecture CJP delivered on February 13, 2001 in the SC Session Hall, surveying how the Court used 'old but reliable doctrines' to meet new e-age paradigms across four domains. His premise, anchored in Judge Learned Hand, is that judges need both liberal education and legal expertise -- 'it is no longer enough for judges to be walking encyclopedias of the Constitution.' On the new economy (globalization, liberalization, deregulation, privatization): Tanada v. Angara upheld WTO membership on grave-abuse deference, holding the 'Filipino First' provisions non-self-executing and the Constitution interpretable for 'future and unknown circumstances'; Manila Prince Hotel was distinguished as a self-executing exception; Tatad v. Secretary of Energy voided the Oil Deregulation Law (RA 8180) 9-2 for entrenching the Petron-Shell-Caltex oligopoly ('the Constitution mandates this Court to be the guardian not only of the people's political rights but their economic rights as well'), while Garcia v. Corona upheld the corrected RA 8479; and Pimentel v. Aguirre affirmed LGU fiscal autonomy. On constitutional and political law he canvasses free expression (ABS-CBN v. Comelec protecting exit polls; Vasquez's actual-malice libel standard), the death penalty (his Dissent in People v. Echegaray that the 1987 Constitution abolished rather than suspended capital punishment and that executions are 'nightmarishly irreversible'), due process for workers (his Serrano Dissent that due process binds private power, not just government) and extraditees (Lantion), privacy (Ople v. Torres), citizenship (Frivaldo; Mercado on dual citizenship; the 'reluctant hinges'), automated elections (Loong; Bush v. Gore), initiative/referendum/recall (Santiago and PIRMA finding RA 6735 inadequate to amend the Constitution), the party-list four parameters (Veterans Federation Party v. Comelec -- 'the Philippine style party list system is a unique paradigm,' rejecting the German Niemeyer formula because 'one cannot grow Washington apples in the Philippines'), and the environment (Oposa; Tano). He treats the Court's role in swearing in President Arroyo on January 20, 2001 only guardedly under the sub judice rule, and closes on medical-malpractice res ipsa loquitur (Batiquin; Ramos). His epilogue concedes the Court has yet to catch up on the death penalty and private-power due process, but credits the 1987 Constitution as 'a beacon of light and a rock of stability,' ending on his Tanada paean that a Constitution 'can withstand the assaults of bigots and infidels but at the same time bend with the refreshing winds of change.'
